sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 490 BCE an Achaemenid expedition under Datis and Artaphernes crossed the Aegean and reached Attica.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The expedition sought to subdue Athens and Eretria. These were imperial objectives, wider than a single battlefield.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Athens needed to preserve its independence; the expedition needed political submission as well as military success.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Marathon was a coastal plain in northeastern Attica. Herodotus describes it as suitable for cavalry.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Athenian and Plataean infantry opposed the Persian expedition. Athenian command included Miltiades and the polemarch Callimachus.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Herodotus describes stronger Greek wings and a shallower center. This is a literary account, not a surveyed deployment.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The narrative moves from an advance to fighting in the center, success on the wings, and a struggle near the ships.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Committing to battle involved accepting risk without certainty about Persian intentions. The surviving narrative cannot recover a commander's private reasoning.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Greek wings prevailed while their center gave ground; the wings then converged against the remaining Persian troops.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Persian force withdrew by sea. The Athenians returned to protect Athens.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The battle became a durable civic memory: the Marathon museum preserves finds associated with the Athenian and Plataean burial mounds.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Compare battlefield success with the continuing task of defending the city. A successful engagement does not remove every operational threat.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Persian cavalry activity and exact troop positions are unresolved here. Accounts of Datis's fate conflict; a schematic must not imply certainty.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Read Herodotus as a later Greek narrative, Iranica for Datis and source criticism, and the archaeological museum for material context.

phases.title: Opposing armies
phases.description: The expedition and Greek defenders face one another on the Marathon plain.

phases.title: Center under pressure
phases.description: In Herodotus's account, the Persian center advances against the thinner Greek center.

phases.title: Wings converge
phases.description: The successful Greek wings turn toward the remaining enemy.

phases.title: Return to Athens
phases.description: The defenders return while the Persian fleet sails around the coast.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Cannae followed Roman defeats at the Trebia and Lake Trasimene during Hannibal's invasion of Italy.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Fabius had avoided favorable battle conditions for Hannibal. The consuls of 216 BCE instead commanded a major concentration of Roman forces.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Rome sought a decisive battlefield recovery; Hannibal sought another defeat severe enough to weaken Roman resistance.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The armies fought near the Aufidus river in Apulia. Livy emphasizes ground favorable to cavalry.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Hannibal commanded African, Iberian, Celtic and Numidian contingents. Roman consuls were Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Polybius describes a projecting Iberian-Celtic center with African infantry on either side; both armies placed cavalry on their wings.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Cavalry fighting accompanied the infantry collision. Roman pressure bent Hannibal's center inward before the Africans attacked the Roman flanks.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Concentration against the enemy center made sense as a breakthrough attempt, but success there did not guarantee security on the flanks.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Victorious Carthaginian cavalry returned against the Roman rear while infantry closed from the sides.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Roman army suffered a catastrophic defeat. Paullus died; Varro survived.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Rome continued the war. Livy's epitome records emergency recruitment and the refusal to ransom prisoners.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Cannae separates tactical achievement from strategic resolution: destroying an army did not compel the Roman state to surrender.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Ancient casualty totals differ. Livy's hostile portrayal of Varro should not be treated as a neutral record of responsibility or private motives.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Polybius supplies the core battle narrative. Livy provides another tradition; the Cambridge introduction contextualizes the preceding campaign.

phases.title: Formation
phases.description: The opposing infantry centers and cavalry wings deploy.

phases.title: Roman advance
phases.description: The Roman infantry presses into the Iberian-Celtic center.

phases.title: Envelopment
phases.description: African infantry turns inward; cavalry threatens the Roman rear.

phases.title: Army defeated
phases.description: Roman resistance collapses, but Rome continues the war.

perspectives.name: Hannibal Barca
perspectives.known: His own army combined infantry contingents with strong cavalry.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the center could remain coherent under pressure.
perspectives.constraints: A multinational army required coordination across separate arms.
perspectives.decision: The ancient narratives describe a yielding center and attacks from the flanks. This explanation reconstructs the plan; it is not a surviving order.

perspectives.name: Gaius Terentius Varro and Lucius Aemilius Paullus
perspectives.objective: Bring Hannibal to a decisive engagement.
perspectives.known: Rome had assembled a large infantry force after earlier defeats.
perspectives.uncertainty: The effect of Hannibal's deployment and the cavalry contest.
perspectives.constraints: Shared consular command and pressure to reverse Roman losses.
perspectives.decision: They fought a pitched battle. Livy assigns the initiative to Varro, but his moral contrast between the consuls requires caution.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 52 BCE Vercingetorix's forces occupied Alesia during the resistance to Caesar's conquest of Gaul.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Caesar's account presents Roman command from the conqueror's perspective. Political self-presentation shapes the narrative.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Romans sought surrender by siege; the defenders awaited a relief army.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Caesar describes a hilltop settlement, nearby rivers, a plain and surrounding heights. The museum interprets the site at Alise-Sainte-Reine.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Caesar directed Roman legions and cavalry; Vercingetorix led the besieged force. Several Gallic leaders shared command of the relief army.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Roman works faced both the settlement and the approaching relief force.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Investment was followed by relief attempts, attacks from inside and outside, and the defeat of the relieving army.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Caesar reports moving reserves to threatened sectors and sending cavalry around the outer works.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: In his narrative, Roman reinforcement and a cavalry attack in the rear broke the final external assault.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Vercingetorix surrendered. Caesar distributed many prisoners as enslaved captives.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The result strengthened Roman domination while imposing conquest and captivity on the defeated population.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Study siege engineering together with food supply and coordination. Static fortifications still required decisions about mobile reserves.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Enemy numbers and dramatic speeches come from Caesar's interested account. The displayed phases simplify an extended siege, not a measured hour-by-hour reconstruction.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Caesar supplies the principal narrative; museum archaeology and landscape interpretation provide a different kind of evidence.

phases.title: Investment
phases.description: Roman works close around Alesia.

phases.title: Double front
phases.description: The Romans prepare to defend against forces outside and inside.

phases.title: Relief assaults
phases.description: The relief army attacks while the besieged attempt sorties.

phases.title: Surrender
phases.description: Vercingetorix is surrendered and the defenders lose their freedom.

sources.title: History of Battle Abbey and Battlefield

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Edward the Confessor's death opened a disputed succession. Harold became king; William of Normandy claimed the crown.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Harold defeated the Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge before returning south to face William's landing in Sussex.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: William needed to defeat the reigning king to advance his claim. Harold needed to contain an invader while preserving royal authority.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The English held a ridge near the modern town of Battle. The battlefield's exact extent remains uncertain.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Harold's army fought on foot, including household warriors. William's army used infantry, archers and mounted troops.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The English occupied the ridge in a defensive formation; William's forces approached from rising ground to the south.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Repeated assaults lasted throughout 14 October 1066. A Norman retreat and rally preceded renewed attacks.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: William rallied his troops after a report that he had died. English pursuit during retreats exposed parts of their formation.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The interaction of lost cohesion and repeated pressure matters more than explaining the result through a single weapon.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Harold was killed and his army broken. William was crowned on Christmas Day.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The victory opened the Norman conquest and transformed England's political relationship with continental Europe.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Distinguish an army's tactical position from the wider demands of defending a kingdom against successive invasions.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The Bayeux Tapestry and written narratives leave details unresolved. This account does not specify Harold's exact fatal wound or precise unit positions.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: English Heritage summarizes the narrative and material setting. Historic England documents the registered battlefield and surviving source problems.

phases.title: The ridge
phases.description: Harold's infantry holds the higher ground.

phases.title: Assault and rally
phases.description: William's forces attack; the duke restores confidence during a retreat.

phases.title: Repeated pressure
phases.description: Further attacks and pursuits disrupt sections of the English formation.

phases.title: Collapse
phases.description: Harold's death accompanies the defeat of his army.

sources.title: 2 décembre 1805 : La bataille d'Austerlitz
sources.publisher: French Ministry of the Armed Forces

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The 1805 campaign carried the Grande Armée from the Channel camps through the Ulm campaign and into Austria.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Austria and Russia confronted Napoleon within the Third Coalition. The battle took place on 2 December 1805 in present-day Czechia.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Napoleon sought a decisive result before the coalition could improve its position. The Allies attempted to turn the French right.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Pratzen Heights dominated the battlefield; Telnitz and Sokolnitz lay in the southern sector.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: French corps under commanders including Soult, Davout and Lannes faced a combined Austro-Russian army.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Allied formations occupied the heights before moving substantial forces south against Napoleon's right.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The southern fighting developed first. Soult then attacked the weakened center, followed by fighting for the plateau and an Allied retreat.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon committed Soult against the Pratzen Heights as Allied troops moved away.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Control of the center divided the coalition's fight and allowed the French to redirect forces against its southern wing.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The French won decisively. Austria signed an armistice on 6 December.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Treaty of Pressburg followed on 26 December, reshaping the political settlement after the campaign.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A useful study question is how timing, terrain and concentration interacted. A deliberate risk can only be assessed against the forces available to support it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The popular image of a perfectly controlled trap compresses a contested battle. This overview omits disputed losses and exact minute-by-minute timing.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Fondation Napoléon timeline and site guide supply sequence and geography. The French Army page represents an institutional commemorative interpretation.

phases.title: Allied movement south
phases.description: Allied forces advance toward Telnitz and Sokolnitz.

phases.title: Assault on Pratzen
phases.description: Soult's corps attacks the weakened Allied center.

phases.title: Contest for the center
phases.description: Counterattacks fail to restore Allied control of the plateau.

phases.title: Allied withdrawal
phases.description: The divided Allied army retreats; French forces press its southern wing.

sources.title: Sketch of the Battle of Waterloo

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Napoleon returned from Elba in 1815. A new coalition mobilized against him.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: His advance into Belgium sought to separate Wellington's and Blücher's armies before larger coalition forces arrived.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The French needed a rapid decision; the Allies needed to sustain cooperation despite separate command structures.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Wellington held the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge with forward strongpoints including Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon faced Wellington's multinational army and, later, Blücher's Prussian corps.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Much Allied infantry sheltered behind the ridge. The surviving archival sketch also identifies infantry squares and the Prussian approach.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Attacks on the strongpoints and center were followed by cavalry assaults, Prussian intervention and the final Guard attack.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Wellington chose to stand with promised Prussian support. Blücher marched toward him after the defeat at Ligny.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Prussian pressure forced Napoleon to divide attention and reserves. The Imperial Guard's repulse preceded general French retreat.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The coalition won on 18 June. Napoleon's attempt to restore his rule failed.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The campaign ended with Allied occupation of Paris and Napoleon's final exile.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Coalition cooperation can be an operational capability. Study liaison and marching decisions alongside the actions visible on the battlefield.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: National narratives assign credit differently. The schematic simplifies simultaneous engagements and does not reproduce archival coordinates.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Compare the National Army Museum narrative with Royal Armouries, the Prussian-focused Fondation dossier and an archival map.

phases.title: Strongpoints attacked
phases.description: French assaults begin against Wellington's forward positions.

phases.title: Assaults on the ridge
phases.description: Infantry and cavalry fighting tests the Allied line.

phases.title: A second front
phases.description: Prussian forces enter the battle against Napoleon's right.

phases.title: Final repulse
phases.description: The Guard attack fails; the Allied advance and pursuit follow.

perspectives.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
perspectives.objective: Defeat Wellington before the coalition armies could combine effectively.
perspectives.known: Ligny had forced a Prussian retreat, but its direction and recovery remained critical.
perspectives.uncertainty: How much Prussian force could reach the battlefield in time.
perspectives.constraints: Wet ground, elapsed time and competing demands for reserves.
perspectives.decision: He continued the attack while allocating troops to the Prussian threat. The account describes actions, not an invented inner monologue.

perspectives.name: Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington
perspectives.objective: Hold the position until Prussian assistance could make a combined victory possible.
perspectives.known: Blücher had promised support; his arrival depended on a difficult march.
perspectives.uncertainty: The timing and scale of reinforcement.
perspectives.constraints: A mixed army, an extended defensive line and repeated French pressure.
perspectives.decision: He defended the ridge and strongpoints, then advanced as the French attack failed.

perspectives.name: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher
perspectives.objective: Restore cooperation with Wellington after Ligny.
perspectives.known: Wellington intended to fight near Waterloo.
perspectives.uncertainty: March delays and the situation when each corps arrived.
perspectives.constraints: Reorganization after defeat and routes from Wavre.
perspectives.decision: He committed corps toward Waterloo. Their intervention turned a two-army encounter into a coalition victory.

sources.title: Major Fleet-versus-Fleet Operations in the Pacific War, 1941–1945

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After rapid Japanese expansion, the Combined Fleet planned an operation against Midway in June 1942.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Yamamoto hoped to draw American carriers into a decisive engagement. U.S. intelligence identified Midway as the principal objective.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Japan sought a favorable fleet battle; Nimitz sought to protect Midway while exploiting advance warning.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The engagement spread across open ocean around the atoll. Scouting aircraft connected widely separated forces.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Nagumo led four Japanese fleet carriers. Fletcher and Spruance commanded three American carriers under Nimitz's operational direction.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: American carrier groups waited northeast of Midway; the Japanese carrier force approached to support the island attack.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The 4 June island strike was followed by unsuccessful American attacks, devastating dive-bomber strikes and Japanese counterattacks.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Fletcher authorized Spruance's early strike while retaining aircraft pending better information. Nagumo faced conflicting demands to rearm aircraft and recover the island strike.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: American dive bombers disabled three Japanese carriers in the morning; Hiryu was mortally damaged later that day.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Japan abandoned the invasion. Four Japanese carriers and the American Yorktown were lost.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The result materially altered the carrier balance, but did not end the Pacific War.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Intelligence created opportunity without removing uncertainty. Scouting, carrier deck operations, navigation and command decisions shaped whether it could be exploited.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: A simple luck-versus-genius explanation obscures interacting causes. The schematic illustrates sequence, not verified ship tracks.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: NHHC provides chronology and intelligence context; the Naval War College study supports analysis of command decisions and incomplete information.

phases.title: Midway attacked
phases.description: Japanese carrier aircraft strike the atoll.

phases.title: Search and launch
phases.description: American aircraft attack; both sides act on incomplete contact reports.

phases.title: Carrier crisis
phases.description: Dive bombers inflict fatal damage on Akagi, Kaga and Soryu.

phases.title: Counterattack and withdrawal
phases.description: Hiryu counterattacks before its loss; Japan withdraws and Yorktown is subsequently lost.

perspectives.name: Chester W. Nimitz and the American carrier command
perspectives.objective: Defend Midway and attack the approaching carrier force.
perspectives.known: Communications intelligence indicated the objective, approximate timing and force.
perspectives.uncertainty: Contact reports did not initially locate every enemy carrier.
perspectives.constraints: Three carriers, aircraft range and the time needed to launch and recover strikes.
perspectives.decision: Nimitz concentrated carriers near Midway; Fletcher and Spruance launched attacks based on scouting reports. These were decisions under uncertainty, not omniscient ambush management.

perspectives.name: Chūichi Nagumo
perspectives.objective: Support the Midway operation while retaining capacity to strike enemy ships.
perspectives.known: The first attack reported a need for another island strike; later scouting identified American ships.
perspectives.uncertainty: The enemy's carrier strength and immediate intentions.
perspectives.constraints: Rearming, landing returning aircraft and defending the carriers competed for time.
perspectives.decision: He ordered preparations for another island strike before new contact information changed the situation. Reasons are reconstructed from operational records rather than private thoughts.

sources.title: A Soviet mortar team advance at Stalingrad, 1942

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Germany's 1942 southern offensive aimed toward the Caucasus oilfields and the Volga region after the failure to defeat the Soviet Union in 1941.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Army Group South was divided, creating competing demands between the Caucasus and Stalingrad.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The campaign combined resource objectives with control of a major transport corridor. Reducing it to a contest over the city's name is inadequate.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Stalingrad extended along the Volga. The surrounding steppe remained essential to the wider battle.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Paulus commanded the German Sixth Army. Soviet defense included the 62nd Army under Chuikov; Romanian formations held exposed sectors outside the city.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: German forces advanced toward the Volga while Soviet forces defended the approaches and then the urban area.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The campaign moved from the summer advance through urban fighting to Operation Uranus and the destruction of the encircled force.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Soviet learning and organizational reform helped make the counteroffensive possible; no single commander's personality adequately explains it.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The November Soviet offensive broke through the flanks and encircled the Sixth Army.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The remaining German forces surrendered by 2 February 1943.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The defeat damaged German strategic prospects and became a major psychological turning point.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Examine an urban battlefield inside its operational setting. Tactical advances through a city can coexist with growing vulnerability outside it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: German and Soviet postwar narratives both simplified responsibility. Casualty totals depend on whether they cover the city, encirclement or wider campaign.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National WWII Museum emphasizes Soviet adaptation; USHMM places the defeat in the war's broader course. NAM supplies additional operational context.

phases.title: Advance to the Volga
phases.description: German forces push toward Stalingrad amid Soviet resistance.

phases.title: Urban battle
phases.description: Fighting narrows the Soviet foothold but does not end resistance.

phases.title: Operation Uranus
phases.description: Soviet attacks against the flanks encircle the German army.

phases.title: Final surrender
phases.description: The encircled force is defeated in separate pockets.
